en: // Prologue //
Salutations to the venerable Śrīmad Bhagavad Rāmānuja.
Salutations to the illustrious Great Preceptor of the Vedānta.

This jewel of a treatise titled *Nyāyapariśuddhi*, which has come forth as a transformation from the successive waves of the river of wisdom of the venerable teacher Veṅkaṭanātha Maṇi, triumphs as the very life of the science of Nyāya-vistara and of the scripture of Brahma-mīmāṃsā, whose path was trodden by the illustrious and noble sage Rāmānuja.
If this branch of knowledge were not relied upon, what power would there be for even the rest of the collection of branches of knowledge to move forward?
For everything heard in the world, being tossed by doubt and error, remains unstable like a blade of grass struck by a whirlwind; it does not find any firm footing at all.
But when properly established through the examination of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), it stands unshakable, its agitation dispelled, like a solid rock.
And the examination of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇaparīkṣā*) alone is the primary gateway for entering the *Nyāyavistara*.
For those learned in the treatises divide the science into three parts according to the distinctions of grammar (*pada*), logic (*vākya*), and epistemology (*pramāṇa*).
Among these, that which is called "instruction on words" (*śabdānuśāsana*) was composed by Pāṇini and others.

And as for the statement: the Mīmāṃsā-śāstra is twofold, consisting of the determination of the meaning of Vedic sentences preceded by inquiry, and being divided into the two subjects of ritual action (karma) and Brahman.

As for the means of knowledge (pramāṇa): the scripture, designated as "reflection" (manana), is that which, like a female elephant, steadies with the chains of logic (tarka) the mind that is swaying, lacking firm support regarding any objects, and devoid of self-confidence even toward its own nature.
Its other designations include Nyāyavistara, Tarkaśāstra, and so forth.

Although this [system] is primarily concerned with the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), because its ultimate purpose is the discernment of the nature of the objects of cognition (*prameya*) through the operation of those means, it has set its foot upon the object of cognition as well.

While the various disputants—both theists and atheists—who are intent on mutual contradiction, grasp the object of cognition in one way or another according to their own whims, they drag the means of valid cognition hither and thither; thus, the means of valid cognition themselves have become distorted in form.
By their very nature, they have become difficult to grasp;
for when true cognitions are intermingled with fallacious cognitions, they are not easy to distinguish.
Thus, the treatise itself has been defiled, like an eye afflicted by cataracts, having become incapable of discerning the meaning.

Even those such as the followers of the Sugata, the Arhatas, the Kāpilas, the Cārvākas, and the Jaiminīyas— who, while grasping the category of valid cognition characterized by non-perversion, maintain [the system] without deficiency or excess regarding its constituent parts and sub-divisions—

have their minds rendered non-conclusive through various applications; and though they are "those of firm mind," yet due to their conviction in the tradition of their own respective teachings, they cling to one particular position, and out of fear of the exhaustion of their own adherence, they remain full of envy toward other positions even after a long time.
Having labored in various schools (garukula), those who have not attained clarity of intellect are seen wandering about in confusion.

Therefore, for the sake of universal utility, through the relinquishing of faults and the adoption of virtues, the sage Gautama first composed the collection of aphorisms known as the Nyāyadarśana, a distinct system of this extensive logic (nyāyavistara) which is to be studied.

In this work, the means for determining reality through the discrimination between valid and invalid cognition and so forth, as well as the merits and defects that may arise therein, and the distinctions between what is to be adopted and what is to be avoided in formal debates, have been demonstrated in detail.

That *Nyāyadarśana* first divides its subject matter into sixteen categories by means of the opening sūtra on the instruments of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), the objects of knowledge (*prameya*), and so forth, and fulfills its purpose through their critical examination.

In that system, however, the property of being an object of knowledge (*prameyatva*)—being a purely positive (*kevalānvayin*) universal—cannot function as a differentiator because it is common to all categories.
The sage Kaṇāda, by enumerating the entire range of objects of knowledge (*prameya*) into seven distinct categories beginning with substance (*dravya*), has divided them without confusion.

Yet, in this regard, the consumer of grains (*kaṇabhakṣa*)—who treats as categories those things that are not actually categories, namely generality (*sāmānya*), particularity (*viśeṣa*), inherence (*samavāya*), and absence (*abhāva*); who speaks of one thing while it is another; and who neither grasps what is to be grasped nor abandons what is to be abandoned—has led us far astray onto a wrong path.

The Vaiśeṣika position was rejected by the authors of the Brahma-sūtras and others as being contrary to the path of the scriptures (*śāstrapatha*). However, regarding the Nyāya position, thinking that it should not be entirely discarded— since even if it is subject to certain objections, it can be refined through some form of interpretation— they adopted this school after refining it with a few corrections and composed their treatises.
There were certain former teachers, and their works remain today in name alone during these days— for example, the *Nyāyatattva* composed by the venerable Nāthamuni Miśra,
and the *Tattvaratnākara*, the work of the venerable Parāśarabhaṭṭāraka.

The two works known as the *Nyāyasudarśana*— whose authors remain unidentified— and the *Prajñāparitrāṇa*, composed by the venerable Rāmamiśra (the teacher of Śrī Puṇḍarīkākṣa, who himself took refuge at the feet of the venerable Nāthamuni,

the teacher of the venerable Bhagavad-Yāmunācāryas); and furthermore, a certain jewel among treatises which, though not mentioned by name, was accepted by the Ācārya as being the work of the venerable Nārāyaṇamuni.

Furthermore, these works— the *Nyāyakuliśa*, which serves as a treasury for the wealth of his own genius and was composed by the teacher Ātreya Rāmānujācārya (who was both the author’s maternal uncle and the one who bestowed upon him the honorific name Vādihaṃsāmbuvāha)—
were cited here and there by the very same author of the *Nyāyapariśuddhi*.
The examples are cited most extensively;

for whatever sentence or fragment of a sentence has been cited by the Teacher here and there, not even a small portion beyond that is found to have come within the range of vision of the commentators.

The reason that appears here is this: even during the times when the Teacher was present, having reflected upon the precious jewels of the Teacher’s well-spoken words—which are delightful through being neither too concise nor too prolix, which have clear meanings, and which are eternally luminous—the circle of disciples and grand-disciples, though inclined toward the mountain of the Teacher’s proclamation that consists in the tasting of aesthetic flavor and victory over disputants, failed to expand the scripture through successive compositions of commentaries and the like; thus, as time passed, they allowed it to perish in vain.

Among Kumāravedāntācārya and others, as well as certain recent authors who appeared during the past century— being unaware of the historical facts previously established— they have rendered some small service by providing explanations in whatever manner they could.
Alas! Even for this system of the venerable Śrī Bhagavad Rāmānuja, whose every blemish has been washed away without remainder, there is this one lamentable calamity:

that it has been disregarded by certain modern scholars who, though consecrated to the rank of Ācāryas, have spent their youth in the laborious study of common treatises such as those of Kaṇāda and Gautama; and only in their final years, having somehow conceived a thirst for Vedānta, they have found leisure to gather disciples and fulfilled their purpose merely by grasping a few essential texts such as the *Śrībhāṣya*.

The extensive discourses of the ancient masters have now reached a state where they are difficult even to hear. To whom among those devoted to learning does such a destruction of knowledge not cause pain in the mind?
Or rather, enough with brooding over the loss of the compositions of the ancients.
How much of the flow of the honeyed speech of this very teacher has not been poured forth in vain?
For the venerable feet of the masters, who are independent in all systems of thought, there are more than a hundred well-known compositions as pure as necklaces.
These include poems, dramas, and hymns composed in the three languages of Sanskrit, Prakrit, and Dravidian, as well as in Persian and Urdu.

There exist collections of works produced for the welfare of the world, which belong to a fourth category; they are composed in a Dravidian language interspersed with Sanskrit as established by worldly usage and treatises; they are beneficial even to common people and easily grasped even by investigators; they are as pure as a mirror regarding the traditional truths and human goals; they are known as "mani-pravāla" (jewels and corals) due to their fixed audibility; they are designated as "secret" (rahasya); and they are intent upon extracting the essence of the established doctrines.
Among these, first, in the Vedānta section, there is the work named *Tattvaṭīkā*, a commentary on the *Śārīrakamīmāṃsābhāṣya* composed by the venerable Lord Rāmānuja Muni;

adorned with the arrangement of extraordinary and specific meanings, it demonstrates unshakable resolutions that refute all possible objections regarding the three periods of time, and it has emerged from this preeminent teacher, who is like Śiva to Gaṅgā.

And this work, even in its mere first sūtra, appears as a fragment intended only for the mental affliction of those who desire to investigate the knowledge of Vedānta, since its full scope has not yet been perceived. When a jewel among warriors— possessing a brilliant and unimpeded power in diverse battles— suddenly ceases his efforts due to the tyranny of fate without having displayed his full strength before bystanders, whose heart would not grieve, even for one who follows the code of a hero?
This is an illustration regarding the omission in this jewel of a treatise:
some might think that this work was not completed by the Teacher himself;
however, such a claim does not hold here for those who, judging by their own example, assume a limitation on his power in every respect.

Indeed, there are three kinds of authors of compendia in the world. Some favor the world by recording upon leaf-manuscripts and revealing the meanings of various subjects as they have heard them through long labor in the houses of teachers;

others, however, are those whose intellects are naturally as pure as crystal, whose intentions are polished by the manifestation of their superior nature, and who, although all objects of knowledge are clearly reflected in the mirror-surface of their own minds, [compose works] out of a desire to preserve the tradition.

Those who do not abandon the path revealed by the instructions of the Guru, and who possess the specific traditions of the teachings of the Guru, logic, and all means of valid cognition moving simultaneously upon the pathways of the gong-like mind,
are capable of grasping and even composing many subjects with ease and in a single stroke.
Others, however, have the spray of obstacles driven far away by the Lord of All, the Blessed One, who has been propitiated through uninterrupted devotion.

Possessing unimpeded power to experience the various forms of spiritual welfare that culminate in the supreme good (*niḥśreyasa*), and to bring even those who have taken refuge at their own feet to such experiences, these extraordinary authors of literary works— whose majesty is worthy of being reckoned even by the hosts of great sages headed by Vyāsa, Parāśara, and Vālmīki— are situated in the third category;
for the jewels of truth (*prameyaratna*) strung upon the single thread of their singular genius appear ever new, even when studied again and again.
They bring about an indescribable wonder in the hearts of the wise, yet they never become dim like ancient paintings.

It is evident to those who know the truth that the Teacher, who effects the purification of logic (*nyāya*), shines forth like a central gem in a string of pearls across both the second and third stages.
And it is natural for the powerful to carry through to the conclusion what has been begun.

For those whose every activity has as its sole fruit the benefit of the world, how could there be an interruption of their intended undertaking when they have begun an effort for the sake of helping the world that is accomplished without exertion? And who, indeed, knowing [his] power, would believe that a work by one such as this— the crest-jewel of teachers— could be left unfinished and cast aside in the middle while he was beginning to clarify the intellects of his disciples?

Moreover: "This banner of victory, which serves as the crest-ornament for the entire series of the Vedas, is now fastened upon the palace-roofs of the minds of the skillful; it is the record of the twenty-eighth exposition of the *Bhāṣya* of the Lord of Ascetics, according to how it was heard and reflected upon."
Thus, at the beginning of the *Tattvaṭīkā*, the Teacher himself clearly states that he composed this work, the *Tattvaṭīkā*, during the twenty-eighth recitation of his own commentary on the *Bhāṣya*.

Furthermore, in the prologue to the *Saṃkalpasūryodaya*, he says: “In my twentieth year, having mastered various branches of knowledge and having caused the *Śārīrakabhāṣya* to be heard thirty times, the illustrious Veṅkaṭanātha has composed this meaningful drama, beneficial to the ears, for the pleasure of Nātha.”
Thus, by the words of the stage director, it is made known that the exposition of the *Śārīrakabhāṣya* was performed thirty times at the time of the composition of the *Saṃkalpasūryodaya*.
If the exposition of the *Śārīrakabhāṣya* occurred exactly thirty times on that occasion, then the subsequent repetitions of its exposition must have been even more numerous than that.
For the time of Kṛṣṇamiśra’s meeting was indeed the period of the composition of the *Saṃkalpasūryodaya*.

Consequently, in the twenty-eighth cycle, the composition of the *Tattvaṭīkā* occurs earlier than the meeting with Kṛṣṇamiśra. Furthermore, it is understood that the *Tattvaṭīkā* was composed immediately after the *Śatadūṣaṇī*.

For it has been stated by the teachers themselves while introducing the *Tattvaṭīkā*: "The futile adherence of Śaṅkara and others has been cut down in the *Śatadūṣaṇī*; however, the body of the *Śārīraka* [Sūtra] is clearly demonstrated here."
"Thus:
'May there be auspiciousness for that most excellent one, by whom the Śrutaprakāśikā was first protected on the earth and subsequently transmitted to worthy recipients.'"

Thus, it might seem superficially plausible that the Teacher’s (Vedāntadeśika’s) intent in composing the *Maṅgalāśāsana* was merely to reflect upon the *Śrutaprakāśikā*, and that his devotion to expounding it arose from a desire to prevent the completion of the *Tattvaṭīkā*. However, this is not so; for although the author of the *Śrutaprakāśikā*—who was like a force of barbarians crushing [the opposition], who was a fellow student of his own Guru, and who was on the verge of death—requested him to protect and expound that work, and he consented to do so, this did not diminish his own great [status].
The Master will render his effort in composing this treatise in vain;
for the collection of unprecedented topics herein does not have its purpose fulfilled by another work.
This is perfectly evident of itself to those who have exerted themselves in the Master’s own writings.
Even regarding those subjects treated in the extant portions of the *Tattvaṭīkā* currently available, they are not easily found explained elsewhere in the *Śrutaprakāśikā* or in any other work.
Furthermore, while the jewel among treatises on logic known as the *Nyāyakuliśa* was already composed by his own teacher, Vādihaṃsāmbuvāha, the Ācārya himself composed the *Nyāyapariśuddhi*.
Moreover, maintaining silence regarding matters that must necessarily be stated is in no way consistent with the status of being a teacher of the scriptures.
Nor does the revelation of ever-new meanings constitute a slight against the ancient teachers.
Furthermore: "She, whose form is the ornament upon the crest of the entire series of the Vedas, is now being bound to the courtyards of the palaces of hope by those of subtle minds."

Thus, he demonstrates the very promise made at the commencement of the work: that this undertaking of an unprecedented composition is for the purpose of expounding the purport of all the Vedāntas—a purport which has not been fully realized in other texts, which consists of the refinement of the meaning of all the Vedāntas, and which even those of great intelligence have desired to hear from the presence of the Omniscient One himself.
How, then, could it not be brought to completion?

Furthermore, it can be inferred that the teachers accepted the exposition of another's work only after remembering that their own composition, the *Śrutaprakāśikā*, had already gained wide currency at the very time they undertook the defense of that work; such being the case, the reason for the omission of portions of the *Tattvaṭīkā* by later teachers was simply their lack of familiarity with it, and not the fact that the work was incomplete.

For just as the *Nyāyasiddhāñjana* is currently seen to terminate merely with the determination of insentient substances (*jaḍadravya*), while the determination of non-substances (*adravya*) has indeed been omitted;
and that [omission] cannot be filled by others.

Thus, regarding this very point, Śrī Raṅgarāmānuja himself stated in his commentary on the *Nyāyasiddhāñjana*: "Therefore, nowhere else has anything been seen beyond this; the work of filling the remainder of that [text] would only be a cause for ridicule.
Whatever else remains to be known has been correctly determined by them in other works; thus, there is nothing here further to be considered."
Concluding thus, he reports:
"Indeed, even the *Śatadūṣaṇī* is not seen in its entirety;
only sixty-six arguments circulate in the world."

As for the remainder, however, some prattle on, having fabricated some entirely false tradition; they claim that this portion of the text, which is devoted to refuting the Dvaita doctrine, was requested with humility by a certain ascetic adhering to the Madhva school who had come to him while wandering for alms— and that [the teacher] composed it for him— but even that is not worthy of critical examination.
For nowhere in the works of the Ācārya is the Madhva doctrine refuted;
this is because there is no subversion of the fundamental truth,
and regarding secondary matters, he merely restates the duality already propounded by the Naiyāyikas, Vaiśeṣikas, and others.
Because that doctrine is not very widespread and because it does not entail the subversion of the world, the teachers would likely have no concern for it;
therefore, the claim that the *Catustriṃśaddvāda* is solely intent upon refuting the Madhva school is merely hearsay.

Furthermore, it becomes clear from the very opening of that work itself that the *Śatadūṣaṇī* was composed precisely for the purpose of refuting the interpretations of the Sūtras and other matters established by Śaṅkara and others.

For therein it is said: “Having followed the path previously seen by the King of Yogis (Yatirāja), or resorting to a doctrine closely related to it, you wise ones, reciting this as taught like parrots, must strive everywhere for the victory over the disguised Buddhists.”
Thus it was promised.
Here, by the statement "or [the view] that relies on a doctrine closely approximating that," the dualists are brought over to one's own side;
and it is also shown that the purpose for undertaking this treatise is precisely the refutation of non-dualism.

And so it is said by the teachers, while pronouncing a verdict in the dispute between Vidyāraṇya and Akṣobhyamuni: "With the sword 'That thou art' (tattvamasi), which cleaves the Supreme and the individual soul, Akṣobhyamuni cut down the great forest of Vidyāraṇya."
Thus it has been stated.

Regarding the verse, "The foolish adherence of Śaṅkara and others has been refuted by the *Śatadūṣaṇī*," it is established that the word "others" (*ādi*) in the phrase "Śaṅkara and others" is intended to include Yādava and Bhāskara.
Therefore, it is clear that the reason modern teachers have not seen the complete text is the interruption of the oral tradition, which is the cause for the loss of the treatise.
In this context, we shall briefly introduce an incidental account of the Master’s meeting with Kṛṣṇamiśra.
For Kṛṣṇamiśra was a native of the Gauḍa country, a crest-jewel among scholars who had applied himself with particular diligence to all branches of knowledge and the arts;
he was a poet who adhered to the doctrine of the non-duality of Brahman (*brahmādvaita*) and, appearing victorious, wandered through all directions out of a desire for debate.
He proceeded gradually toward the southern direction.

Having heard that Śrīraṅga was a divine field and the abode of the wise, he approached the temple of the Lord Śrīraṅgarāja under the pretext of seeking service to the deity, while requesting a contest of debate.
At that time, having heard vernacular verses being sung there with passion and rhythm, as well as [the works] of the poets who composed them—

Having observed that even images of those of lower castes were being worshipped in that temple with the same ritual offerings as the gods, he summoned the Śrīvaiṣṇavas who were assembled there for service—
men advanced in knowledge— and addressed them: "O wise ones, by this recitation of corrupt speech and this worship of those of lower castes, the Vaiṣṇava splendor has been driven far away."
"What is the use of this propitiation? For what has been done otherwise becomes as if undone," he asked with reproach;
yet when those who had gathered together could not provide any reply befitting his reproach, [he continued].
Having reported that matter to the local ruler of that region at that very time,

and having enjoined him that "all renovations of the temple, beginning with its consecration, must be carried out as if it were brand new," he caused that divine temple to have its doors secured with firmly fixed bolts and all its worship and festivals suspended.
Lokācārya and many others who were spiritual preceptors there, reflecting upon such an unimaginable calamity that had befallen them,

sank into a sea of sorrow difficult to endure; and perceiving their opponent to be an expert in all branches of knowledge, a hero invincible in the arena of debate, they convened an entirely new assembly and deliberated on some means to counteract that misfortune.

In that great assembly of scholars, the illustrious Lokācārya, the preceptor of the tradition, whose words were heeded by all the members of the council, took up a capable and worthy speech: "O sirs, a certain means occurs to me here to turn back our powerful adversary; let it be heard and approved by you as it is being stated."
It is said that in the city of Kāñcī there was a man named Veṅkaṭanāthārya, the foremost among the learned.
For it is the conviction of those who know the truth that he was indeed an incarnation of a portion of Ghaṇṭānātha, the Lord of Vṛṣaśaila.
While still a child of about five years of age, he was taken by his maternal uncle, Ātreya Rāmānujācārya, who was like a cloud to the swans of debate.
While traveling to the presence of Varadaguru to receive the Śārīrakabhāṣya, he was accompanied by his dear nephew; there,

as he untied the many knots of doubt-chains concerning the Bhāṣya that had bound him, he was looked upon with great respect by the assembly of elders gathered there— whose minds were adorned with unprecedented wonder and grace— and by the illustrious Varadaguru himself.

With renewed hope, [the author] says: "May you—who have established the Vedānta and refuted all external doctrines—be honored by those learned in the three Vedas and become a vessel for abundant auspiciousness; for, by divine providence, a support for the doctrine of the venerable Śrī Bhagavad Rāmānuja has now been found."

By offering this benediction— "For this boy, whose essence consists of the meaning of all scriptures intuitively revealed to him by himself, the instruction of a guru will have as its sole fruit the refinement of his learning;
no trace of power regarding knowledge need be instilled in him"—
[it is implied that] even the Blessed Lord, the delighter of Devakī, undertook residence at a teacher's house in the presence of the preceptor Sāndīpani for the sake of acquiring knowledge.
Moreover, this excellence of wisdom in his very childhood, like the extraordinary prowess of Rāma, the son of Daśaratha, is innate from birth;
it is not fitting to bring it within the range of ordinary human vision.
Eyes filled with envy or wonder ought not to fall upon him at such a tender age.
"Indeed, how many men of great virtue have not set like trees consumed by spreading fires of poisonous views? Without having benefited the world with their own qualities, they have passed away.
Only you are capable of making this youth wise in all the scriptures.
Let this victory-banner of the illustrious doctrine of the venerable Rāmānuja be raised! Having spoken thus, the child was entrusted to his maternal uncle, the teacher Vādihaṃsāmbuda.
Then, even while being only about twenty years of age, he became invincible to others due to his awakening that had spread in every direction.

Thus, possessing the wealth of inexhaustible eloquence and being fully competent as a teacher to understand and clarify the unblemished path in all the Tantras, he once [went] to the city of Kāñcī to [visit] the Blessed One, the God of Gods.

During the great festival of the Vaiśākha month procession of the illustrious Devarāja, the author of the *Prabandharatna*, Mādhavācārya— the commentator on the Vedas whose name was celebrated as Vidyāraṇya for his mastery across all branches of learning— arrived out of curiosity to engage in scholarly debate; he stood ready for the battle of disputation against those who rained down a shower of arrows of unrestrained and sharp logic.
Unable to stand before the Ācārya, his mind filled with wonder and great respect, he departed for Vijayanagara.
Having reported the matter exactly as it had occurred to his royal disciple, he set out at the request of the Lord— who was eager to behold such a jewel among scholars—
preceded by the king’s state elephant and augmented by the full royal paraphernalia, including the parasol and fly-whisks.
Having dispatched a fourfold army accompanied by a letter of respectful summons delivered by the hand of his chief minister, he requested the *Vairāgyapañcaka* from him;
and Mādhavācārya, while introducing the Rāmānuja-darśana in his own *Sarvadarśanasaṃgraha*, began with the words: "As stated by Veṅkaṭanātha in the *Tattvamuktākalāpa*," and so forth.
Auspiciousness.
Homage to the glorious Hayavadana, the Supreme Brahman.
Salutations to the illustrious Rāmānuja.
Salutations to the illustrious Great Preceptor of the Upanishads.
May the illustrious Veṅkaṭanātha, the lion among poets and logicians,
the preeminent teacher of Vedānta, dwell forever within my heart.
